body.input: And now here's my conversation with Jitendra Malik.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: In 1966, Seymour Papper at MIT wrote up a proposal called the Summer Vision Project to be given, as far as we know, to 10 students to work on and solve that summer.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: So that proposal outlined many of the computer vision task we still work on today.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: What do you think we underestimate and perhaps we did underestimate and perhaps still underestimate how hard computer vision is?

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: Because most of what we do in vision, we do unconsciously or subconsciously.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: In human vision.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: In human vision. So that gives us this, that effortlessness gives us the sense that, oh, this must be very easy to implement on a computer.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: Now, this is why the early researchers in AI got it so wrong.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: However, if you go into neuroscience or psychology of human vision, then the complexity becomes very clear.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: The fact is that a very large part of the cerebral cortex is devoted to visual processing.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: I mean, and this is true in other primates as well.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: So once we looked at it from a neuroscience or psychology perspective, it becomes quite clear that the problem is very challenging and it will take some time.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: You said the higher level parts are the harder parts.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: I think vision appears to be easy because most of what visual processing is subconscious or unconscious.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: So we underestimate the difficulty. Whereas when you are like proving a mathematical theorem or playing chess, the difficulty is much more evident.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: So because it is your conscious brain which is processing various aspects of the problem solving behavior.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: Whereas in vision, all this is happening, but it's not in your awareness. It's operating below that.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: But it still seems strange. Yes, that's true. But it seems strange that as computer vision researchers, for example,

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: the community broadly is time and time again makes the mistake of thinking the problem is easier than it is.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: Or maybe it's not a mistake. We'll talk a little bit about autonomous driving, for example, how hard of a vision task that is.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: Do you think, I mean, is it just human nature or is there something fundamental to the vision problem that we underestimate?

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: We're still not able to be cognizant of how hard the problem is.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: Yeah, I think in the early days it could have been excused because in the early days all aspects of AI were regarded as too easy.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: But I think today it is much less excusable. And I think why people fall for this is because of what I call the fallacy of the successful first step.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: There are many problems in vision where getting 50% of the solution you can get in one minute.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: Getting to 90% can take you a day. Getting to 99% may take you five years and 99.99% may be not in your lifetime.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: I wonder if that's a unique division. It seems that language people are not so confident about.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: So natural language processing, people are a little bit more cautious about our ability to solve that problem.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: I think for language people intuit that we have to be able to do natural language understanding.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: For vision, it seems that we're not cognizant or we don't think about how much understanding is required.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: It's probably still an open problem. But in your sense, how much understanding is required to solve vision?

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: Put another way, how much something called common sense reasoning is required to really be able to interpret even static scenes?

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: Vision operates at all levels and there are parts which can be solved with what we could call maybe peripheral processing.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: In the human vision literature, there used to be these terms sensation, perception and cognition,

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: which roughly speaking referred to the front end of processing, middle stages of processing and higher level of processing.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: I think they made a big deal out of this and they wanted to study only perception and then dismiss certain problems as being cognitive.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: But really, I think these are artificial divides. The problem is continuous at all levels and there are challenges at all levels.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: The techniques that we have today, they work better at the lower and mid levels of the problem.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: I think the higher levels of the problem, quote, the cognitive levels of the problem are there and in many real applications, we have to confront them.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: Now, how much that is necessary will depend on the application. For some problems, it doesn't matter. For some problems, it matters a lot.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: So I am, for example, a pessimist on fully autonomous driving in the near future.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: And the reason is because I think there will be that 0.01% of the cases where quite sophisticated cognitive reasoning is called for.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: However, there are tasks where you can, first of all, they are much more, they are robust. So in the sense that error rates, error is not so much of a problem.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: For example, let's say you're doing image search. You're trying to get images based on some description, some visual description.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: We are very tolerant of errors there, right? I mean, when Google Image Search gives you some images back and a few of them are wrong, it's okay.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: It doesn't hurt anybody. There's no, there's not a matter of life and death.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: But making mistakes when you are driving at 60 miles per hour and you could potentially kill somebody is much more important.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: So just for the fun of it, since you mentioned, let's go there briefly about autonomous vehicles.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: So one of the companies in the space, Tesla, is with Andhra Kapothi and Elon Musk are working on a system called Autopilot,

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: which is primarily a vision based system with eight cameras and basically a single neural network, a multitask neural network.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: They call it HydroNet, multiple heads. So it does multiple tasks, but is forming the same representation at the core.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: Do you think driving can be converted in this way to purely a vision problem and then solved with learning?

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: Or even more specifically in the current approach, what do you think about what Tesla Autopilot team is doing?

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: So the way I think about it is that there are certainly subsets of the visual based driving problem, which are quite solvable.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: So, for example, driving in freeway conditions is quite a solvable problem.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: I think there were demonstrations of that going back to the 1980s by someone called Ernst Tickman in Munich.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: In the 90s, there were approaches from Carnegie Mellon. There were approaches from our team at Berkeley.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: In the 2000s, there were approaches from Stanford and so on. So autonomous driving in certain settings is very doable.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: The challenge is to have an autopilot work under all kinds of driving conditions.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: At that point, it's not just a question of vision or perception, but really also of control and dealing with all the edge cases.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: So where do you think most of the difficult cases? To me, even the highway driving is an open problem because it applies the same 50, 90, 95, 99 rule.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: Or the fallacy of the first step, I forget how you put it, we fall victim to.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: I think even highway driving has a lot of elements because to solve autonomous driving, you have to completely relinquish the help of a human being.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: You're always in control. So you're really going to feel the edge cases.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: So I think even highway driving is really difficult.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: But in terms of the general driving task, do you think vision is the fundamental problem or is it also your action, the interaction with the environment, the ability to?

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: And then like the middle ground, I don't know if you put that under vision, which is trying to predict the behavior of others, which is a little bit in the world of understanding the scene.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: But it's also trying to form a model of the actors in the scene and predict their behavior.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: Yeah, I include that in vision because to me, perception blends into cognition and building predictive models of other agents in the world, which could be other agents, could be people, other agents, could be other cars.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: That is part of the task of perception because perception always has to not tell us what is now, but what will happen.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: Because what's now is boring. It's done. It's over with.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: We care about the future because we act in the future.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: And we care about the past in as much as it informs what's going to happen in the future.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: So I think we have to build predictive models of behaviors of people and those can get quite complicated.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: So I mean, I've seen examples of this in actually, I mean, I own a Tesla and it has various safety features built in.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: And what I see are these examples where, let's say, there is some skateboarder.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: I mean, I don't want to be too critical because obviously these systems are always being improved and any specific criticism I have, maybe the system six months from now will not have that particular failure mode.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: So it had the wrong response and it's because it couldn't predict what this skateboarder was going to do.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: And because it really required that higher level cognitive understanding of what skateboarders typically do as opposed to a normal pedestrian.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: So what might have been the correct behavior for a pedestrian, a typical behavior for a pedestrian was not the typical behavior for a skateboarder.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: Right. Yeah. And so therefore, to do a good job there, you need to have enough data where you have pedestrians, you also have skateboarders, you've seen enough skateboarders to see what kinds of patterns of behavior they have.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: So it is in principle with enough data that problem could be solved.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: But I think our current systems, computer vision systems, they need far, far more data than humans do for learning those same capabilities.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: So say that there is going to be a system that solves autonomous driving.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: Do you think it will look similar to what we have today, but have a lot more data, perhaps more compute, but the fundamental architectures involved like neural, well, in the case of Tesla autopilot is neural networks.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: Do you think it will look similar in that regard and we'll just have more data?

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: That's a scientific hypothesis as to which way is it going to go.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: I will tell you what I would bet on. So, and this is my general philosophical position on how these learning systems have been.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: What we have found currently very effective in computer vision in the deep learning paradigm is sort of tabular ASA learning and tabular ASA learning in a supervised way with lots and lots of...

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: What's tabular ASA learning?

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: Tabular ASA in the sense that blank slate. We just have the system which is given a series of experiences in this setting and then it learns there.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: Now, if let's think about human driving, it is not tabular ASA learning.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: So at the age of 16 in high school, a teenager goes into driver ed class.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: And now at that point they learn, but at the age of 16, they are already visual geniuses because from 0 to 16, they have built a certain repertoire of vision.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: In fact, most of it has probably been achieved by age 2.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: In this period of age up to age 2, they know that the world is three dimensional.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: They know how objects look like from different perspectives.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: They know about occlusion. They know about common dynamics of humans and other bodies.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: They have some notion of intuitive physics.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: So they have built that up from their observations and interactions in early childhood and of course reinforced through their growing up to age 16.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: So then at age 16, when they go into driver ed, what are they learning?

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: They are not learning afresh the visual world.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: They have a mastery of the visual world.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: What they are learning is control.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: They are learning how to be smooth about control, about steering and brakes and so forth.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: They are learning a sense of typical traffic situations.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: Now, that education process can be quite short because they are coming in as visual geniuses.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: And of course, in their future, they are going to encounter situations which are very novel.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: So during my driver ed class, I may not have had to deal with a skateboarder.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: I may not have had to deal with a truck driving in front of me where the back opens up and some junk gets dropped from the truck and I have to deal with it.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: But I can deal with this as a driver even though I did not encounter this in my driver ed class.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: And the reason I can deal with it is because I have all this general visual knowledge and expertise.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: And do you think the learning mechanisms we have today can do that kind of long term accumulation of knowledge?

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: Or do we have to do some kind of, you know, the work that led up to expert systems with knowledge representation,

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: you know, the broader field of artificial intelligence worked on this kind of accumulation of knowledge.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: Do you think neural networks can do the same?

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: I think I don't see any in principle problem with neural networks doing it.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: But I think the learning techniques would need to evolve significantly.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: So the current learning techniques that we have are supervised learning.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: You're given lots of examples, X, Y, Y pairs, and you learn the functional mapping between them.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: I think that human learning is far richer than that.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: It includes many different components.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: There is a child explores the world and sees, for example, a child takes an object and manipulates it in his or her hand

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: and therefore gets to see the object from different points of view.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: And the child has commanded the movement.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: So that's a kind of learning data, but the learning data has been arranged by the child.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: And this is a very rich kind of data.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: The child can do various experiments with the world.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: So there are many aspects of human learning, and these have been studied in child development by psychologists.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: And what they tell us is that supervised learning is a very small part of it.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: There are many different aspects of learning.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: And what we would need to do is to develop models of all of these and then train our systems with that kind of protocol.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: So new methods of learning, some of which might imitate the human brain.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: But you also in your talks have mentioned sort of the compute side of things in terms of the difference in the human brain

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: or referencing Hans Marvac.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: So do you think there's something interesting, valuable to consider about the difference in the computational power of the human brain

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: versus the computers of today in terms of instructions per second?

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: Yes. So if we go back, so this is a point I've been making for 20 years now.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: And I think once upon a time, the way I used to argue this was that we just didn't have the computing power of the human brain.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: Our computers were not quite there.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: And there is a well-known trade-off, which we know that neurons are slow compared to transistors,

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: but we have a lot of them and they have a very high connectivity.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: Whereas in silicon, you have much faster devices, transistors switch at the order of nanoseconds,

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: but the connectivity is usually smaller.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: At this point in time, I mean, we are now talking about 2020, we do have, if you consider the latest GPUs and so on, amazing computing power.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: And if we look back at Hans Marvac's type of calculations, which he did in the 1990s, we may be there today in terms of computing power comparable to the brain,

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: but it's not of the same style. It's of a very different style.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: So, I mean, for example, the style of computing that we have in our GPUs is far, far more power hungry than the style of computing that is there in the human brain or other biological entities.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: Yeah, and that the efficiency part is we're going to have to solve that in order to build actual real-world systems of large scale.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: Let me ask sort of the high level question, taking a step back.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: How would you articulate the general problem of computer vision? Does such a thing exist?

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: So if you look at the computer vision conferences and the work that's been going on, it's often separated into different little segments,

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: breaking the problem of vision apart into segmentation, 3D reconstruction, object detection, I don't know, image captioning, whatever.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: There's benchmarks for each. But if you were to sort of philosophically say, what is the big problem of computer vision? Does such a thing exist?

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: Yes, but it's not in isolation. So for all intelligence tasks, I always go back to sort of biology or humans.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: And if you think about vision or perception in that setting, we realize that perception is always to guide action.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: Perception for a biological system does not give any benefits unless it is coupled with action.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: So we can go back and think about the first multicellular animals which arose in the Cambrian era, you know, 500 million years ago.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: And these animals could move and they could see in some way. And the two activities helped each other.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: Because how does movement help? Movement helps that because you can get food in different places.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: But you need to know where to go. And that's really about perception or seeing.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: I mean, vision is perhaps the single most perception sense, but all the others are equally are also important.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: So perception and action kind of go together. So earlier it was in these very simple feedback loops which were about finding food or avoiding becoming food if there's a predator running, trying to eat you up and so forth.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: So we must at the fundamental level connect perception to action.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: Then as we evolved, perception became more and more sophisticated because it served many more purposes.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: And so today we have what seems like a fairly general purpose capability which can look at the external world and build a model of the external world inside the head.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: We do have that capability. That model is not perfect. And psychologists have great fun in pointing out the ways in which the model in your head is not a perfect model of the external world.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: They create various illusions to show the ways in which it is imperfect.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: But it's amazing how far it has come from a very simple perception action loop that exists in an animal 500 million years ago.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: Once we have these very sophisticated visual systems, we can then impose a structure on them.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: It's we as scientists who are imposing that structure where we have chosen to characterize this part of the system as this quote module of object detection or quote this module of 3D reconstruction.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: What's going on is really all of these processes are running simultaneously and they are running simultaneously because originally their purpose was in fact to help guide action.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: So as a guiding general statement of a problem, do you think we can say that the general problem of computer vision, you said in humans it was tied to action.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: Do you think we should also say that ultimately the goal, the problem of computer vision is to sense the world in a way that helps you act in the world?

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: Yes, I think that's the most fundamental purpose.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: We have by now hyper evolved.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: So we have this visual system which can be used for other things.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: For example, judging the aesthetic value of a painting.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: And this is not guiding action.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: Maybe it's guiding action in terms of how much money you will put in your auction bid, but that's a bit stretched.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: But the basics are in fact in terms of action.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: But we have evolved really this hyper, we have hyper evolved our visual system.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: Actually, just to sorry to interrupt, but perhaps it is fundamentally about action.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: You kind of jokingly said about spending, but perhaps the capitalistic drive that drives a lot of the development in this world is about the exchange of money.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: The fundamental action is money.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: If you watch Netflix, if you enjoy watching movies, you're using your perception system to interpret the movie.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: Ultimately, your enjoyment of that movie means you'll subscribe to Netflix.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: So the action is this extra layer that we've developed in modern society perhaps is fundamentally tied to the action of spending money.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: Well, certainly with respect to interactions with firms.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: So in this homo economicus role when you're interacting with firms, it does become that.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: What else is there?

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: That was a rhetorical question.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: So to to linger on the division between the static and the dynamic, so much of the work in computer vision, so many of the breakthroughs that you've been a part of have been in the static world.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: In looking at static images.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: And then you've also worked on starting, but it's a much smaller degree.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: The community is looking at dynamic and video at dynamics.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: And then there is robotic vision, which is dynamic, but also where you're actually have a robot in the physical world interacting based on that vision.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: Which problem is harder?

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: The the the the sort of the the trivial first answers of course one image is harder.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: But if you look at a deeper question there, are we, what's the term, cutting ourselves cutting ourselves at the knees or like making the problem harder by focusing on images.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: That's a fair question.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: I think sometimes we we can simplify a problem so much that we essentially lose part of the juice that could enable us to solve the problem.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: And one could reasonably argue that, to some extent, this happens when we go from video to single images.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: Now, historically, you have to consider the limits of imposed by the competition capabilities we had.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: So if we many of the choices made in the computer vision community through the 70s, 80s, 90s can be understood as choices which were forced upon us by the fact that we just didn't have access to compute enough compute.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: Not enough memory, not enough hardware.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: Exactly. Not enough, not enough compute, not enough storage.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: So, so think of these choices. So one of the choices is focusing on single images rather than video.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: Okay.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: Clear questions, storage and compute.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: We had to focus on, we did, we used to detect edges and throw away the image.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: Right. So you have an image, which I say 256 by 256 pixels. And instead of keeping around the grayscale value.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: What we did was we detected edges, find the places where the brightness changes a lot.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: So now that's, and now, and then throw away the rest. So this was a major compression device.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: And the hope was that this makes it that you can still work with it. And the logic was humans can interpret a line drawing.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: And, and yes, and this will save us a competition. So many of the choices were dictated by that.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: I think today we are no longer detecting edges. Right.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: We process images with coordinates because we don't need to. We don't have that, those compute restrictions anymore.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: Now video is still understudied because video compute is still quite challenging.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: If you are a university researcher, I think video computing is not so challenging if you are at Google or Facebook or Amazon.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: Still super challenging. I've just spoke with the VP of engineering, Google, head of the YouTube search and discovery.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: And they still struggle doing stuff on video. It's very difficult except doing, except using techniques that are essentially the techniques you use in the nineties.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: Some very basic computer vision techniques.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: No, that's when you want to do things at scale.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: So if you want to operate at the scale of all the content of YouTube, it's very challenging and there are similar issues in Facebook.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: But as a researcher, you have more opportunities.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: You can train large, you know, networks with relatively large video datasets.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: Yes. So I think that this is part of the reason why we have so emphasized static images.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: I think that this is changing and over the next few years, I see a lot more progress happening in video.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: So I have this generic statement that to me, video recognition feels like 10 years behind object recognition.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: And you can quantify that because you can take some of the challenging video datasets and their performance on action classification is like, say, 30 percent,

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: which is kind of what we used to have around 2009 in object detection.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: It's like about 10 years behind. And whether it'll take 10 years to catch up is a different question.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: Hopefully it will take less than that.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: Let me ask a similar question I've already asked. But once again, so for dynamic scenes,

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: do you think do you think some kind of injection of knowledge basis and reasoning is required to help improve like action recognition?

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: Like if if if if we solve the general action recognition problem, what do you think the solution would look like?

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: Yeah, so I I completely agree that knowledge is called for and that knowledge can be quite sophisticated.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: So the way I would say it is that perception blends into cognition and cognition brings in issues of memory and this notion of a schema from psychology,

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: which is let me use the classic example, which is you go to a restaurant right now, the things happen in a certain order.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: You walk in, somebody takes you to a table, waiter comes, gives you a menu, takes the order, food arrives.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: Eventually, the bill arrives, etc, etc.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: This is a classic example of AI from the 1970s. It was called there was the term frames and scripts and schema.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: These are all quite similar ideas. OK, and then in the 70s, the way the AI of the time dealt with it was by hand coding this.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: So they hand coded in this notion of a script and the various stages and the actors and so on and so forth.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: And use that to interpret, for example, language.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: I mean, if there's a description of a of a story involving some people eating at a restaurant,

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: there are all these inferences you can make because you know what happens typically at a restaurant.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: So I think this kind of this kind of knowledge is absolutely essential.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: So I think that when we are going to do long form video understanding, we are going to need to do this.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: I think the kinds of technology that we have right now with 3D convolutions over a couple of seconds of clip or video,

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: it's very much tailored towards short term video understanding, not that long term understanding.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: Long term understanding requires a notion of this notion of schemas that I talked about, perhaps some notions of goals, intentionality, functionality and so on and so forth.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: Now, how will we bring that in? So we could either revert back to the 70s and say, OK, I'm going to hand code in a script or we might try to learn it.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: So I tend to believe that we have to find learning ways of doing this because I think learning ways land up being more robust.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: And there must be a learning version of the story because children acquire a lot of this knowledge by sort of just observation.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: So at no moment in a child's life does it's possible, but I think it's not so typical that somebody that a mother coaches a child through all the stages of what happens in a restaurant.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: They just go as a family. They go to the restaurant, they eat, come back and the child goes through 10 such experiences and the child has got a schema of what happens when you go to a restaurant.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: So we somehow need to we need to provide that capability to our systems.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: You mentioned the following line from the end of the Alan Turing paper, Computing Machinery and Intelligence, that many people, like you said, many people know and very few have read where he proposes the Turing test.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: This is how you know because it's towards the end of the paper.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: Instead of trying to produce a program to simulate the adult mind, why not rather try to produce one which simulates the child's.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: So that's a really interesting point.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: If I think about the benchmarks we have before us, the tests of our computer vision systems, they're often kind of trying to get to the adult.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: So what kind of benchmarks should we have? What kind of tests for computer vision do you think we should have that mimic the child's in computer vision?

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: Yeah, I think we should have those and we don't have those today.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: And I think the part of the challenge is that we should really be collecting data of the type that a child experiences.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: Right. So that gets into issues of privacy and so on and so forth.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: But there are attempts in this direction to sort of try to collect the kind of data that a child encounters growing up.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: So what's the child's linguistic environment? What's the child's visual environment?

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: So if we could collect that kind of data and then develop learning schemes based on that data, that would be one way to do it.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: I think that's a very promising direction myself.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: There might be people who would argue that we could just short circuit this in some way.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: And sometimes we have imitated, we have had success by not imitating nature in detail.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: So the usual example is airplanes, right? We don't build flapping wings.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: So, yes, that's one of the points of debate.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: In my mind, I would bet on this learning like a child approach.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: So one of the fundamental aspects of learning like a child is the interactivity.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: So the child gets to play with the data set it's learning from.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: Yes.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: So it gets to select. I mean, you can call that active learning in the machine learning world.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: You can call it a lot of terms.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: What are your thoughts about this whole space of being able to play with the data set or select what you're learning?

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: Yeah. So I think that I believe in that.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: And I think that we could achieve it in two ways.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: And I think we should use both.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: So one is actually real robotics, right?

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: So real, you know, physical embodiments of agents who are interacting with the world and they have a physical body with dynamics and mass and moment of inertia and friction and all the rest.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: And you learn your body, the robot learns its body by doing a series of actions.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: The second is that simulation environments.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: So I think simulation environments are getting much, much better.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: In my life, in Facebook AI research, our group has worked on something called Habitat, which is a simulation environment, which is a visually photorealistic environment of, you know, places like houses or interiors of various urban spaces and so forth.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: And as you move, you get a picture, which is a pretty accurate picture.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: So I can now you can imagine that subsequent generations of these simulators will be accurate, not just visually, but with respect to, you know, forces and masses and haptic interactions and so on.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: And then then we have that environment to play with.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: I think that let me state one reason why I think this active being able to act in the world is important.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: I think that this is one way to break the correlation versus causation barrier.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: So this is something which is of a great deal of interest these days.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: I mean, people like Judea Pearl have talked a lot about that we are neglecting causality and he describes the entire set of successes of deep learning as just curve fitting.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: Right. Because it's but I don't quite agree.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: He's a troublemaker. He is.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: But causality is important, but causality is not is not like a single silver bullet. It's not like one single principle. There are many different aspects here.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: And one of the ways in which one of our most reliable ways of establishing causal links and this is the way, for example, the medical community does this is randomized control trials.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: So you have you pick some situation and now in some situation you perform an action and for certain others you don't.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: Right. So you have a control experiment. Well, the child is in fact performing controlled experiments all the time.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: Right. Right. Okay. Small scale.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: In a small scale. And but but that is a way that the child gets to build and refine its causal models of the world. And my colleague, Alison Gopnik has together with a couple of authors, co-authors has this book called The Scientist in the Crib, referring to his children.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: So I like the part that I like about that is the scientist wants to do wants to build causal models and the scientist does control experiments.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: And I think the child is doing that. So to enable that, we will need to have these these active experiments.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: And I think this could be done some in the real world and some in simulation.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: So you have hope for simulation.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: I have hope for simulation.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: That's an exciting possibility if we can get to not just photorealistic, but what's that called? Life realistic.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: Simulation. So you don't see any fundamental blocks to why we can't eventually simulate the principles of what it means to exist in the world.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: I don't see any fundamental problems that I mean, and look, the computer graphics community has come a long way. Right. So in the early days back, going back to the 80s and 90s, they were they were focusing on visual realism.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: Right. And then they could do the easy stuff, but they couldn't do stuff like hair or fur and so on.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: OK, well, they managed to do that. Then they couldn't do physical actions. Right. Like there's a bowl of glass and it falls down and it shatters.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: But then they could start to do pretty realistic models of that and so on and so forth.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: So the graphics people have shown that they can do this forward direction, not just for optical interactions, but also for physical interactions.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: So I think, of course, some of that is very compute intensive, but I think by and by, we will find ways of making our models ever more realistic.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: You break vision apart into in one of your presentations, early vision, static scene understanding, dynamics, understanding and raise a few interesting questions.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: I thought I could just throw some some at you to see if you want to talk about them. So early vision. So it's what is it that you said?

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: Sensation, perception and cognition. So is this a sensation? Yes.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: What can we learn from image statistics that we don't already know?

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: So at the lowest level, what can we make from just the statistics, the basics, the variations in the rock pixels, the textures and so on?

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: Yeah. So what we seem to have learned is that there's a lot of redundancy in these images.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: And as a result, we are able to do a lot of compression. And this compression is very important in biological settings.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: And so there are analogs of that which are happening in our neural net, artificial neural networks.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: At the early layers. So you think there's a lot of compression that can be done in the beginning.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: Just the statistics. Yeah.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: How much?

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: So I mean, the way to think about it is just how successful is image compression.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: And that's been done with older technologies, but it can be done with several companies which are trying to use sort of these more advanced neural network type techniques for compression, both for static images as well as for video.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: One of my former students has a company which is trying to do stuff like this.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: And I think that they are showing quite interesting results.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: And I think that that's all the success of that's really about image statistics and video statistics.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: But that's still not doing compression of the kind. When I see a picture of a cat, all I have to say is it's a cat.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: That's another semantic kind of compression.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: Yeah. So this is at the lower level, right? So we are, as I said, yeah, that's focusing on low level statistics.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: So to linger on that for a little bit, you mentioned how far can bottom up image segmentation go?

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: What does bottom up mean, sorry?

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: So it started from the raw pixels?

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: And I'm not happy with either of these choices fully.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: We have gone into, because we have completely separated these processes.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: So I would like the process, so what do we know compared to biology?

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: So in biology, what we know is that the processes at test time, at run time, those processes are not purely feed forward, but they involve feedback.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: And they involve much shallower neural networks.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110
