metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: So there are backward connections.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: And this might enable us to deal with the more ambiguous stimuli, for example.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: So the biological solution seems to involve feedback.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: The solution in artificial vision seems to be just feed forward, but with a much deeper network.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: And the two are functionally equivalent, because if you have a feedback network, which just has like three rounds of feedback,

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: you can just unroll it and make it three times the depth and create it in a totally feed forward way.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: So this is something which, I mean, we have written some papers on this theme,

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: but I really feel that this theme should be pursued further.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: Some kind of recurrence mechanisms.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: Yeah.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: Okay.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: So I want to have a little bit more top down at test time.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: Okay.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: Then at training time, we make use of a lot of top down knowledge right now.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: So basically to learn to segment an object, we have to have all these examples of this is the boundary of a cat,

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: and this is the boundary of a chair, and this is the boundary of a horse, and so on.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: And this is too much top down knowledge.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: How do humans do this?

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: We manage with far less supervision.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: And we do it in a sort of bottom up way, because, for example, we're looking at a video stream and the horse moves.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: And that enables me to say that all these pixels are together.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: So the Gestalt psychologists used to call this the principle of common fate.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: So there was a bottom up process by which we were able to segment out these objects.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: And we have totally focused on this top down training signal.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: So in my view, we have currently solved it in machine vision, this top down bottom up interaction.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: But I don't find the solution fully satisfactory.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: And I would rather have a bit of both at both stages.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: For all computer vision problems, not just segmentation.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: And the question that you can ask is, so for me, I'm inspired a lot by human vision and I care about that.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: You could be just a hard boiled engineer and not give a damn.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: So to you, I would then argue that you would need far less training data if you could make my research agenda fruitful.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: OK, so then maybe taking a step into segmentation, static scene understanding.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: What is the interaction between segmentation and recognition?

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: You mentioned the movement of objects.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: So for people who don't know computer vision, segmentation is this weird activity that computer vision folks have all agreed is very important.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: Of drawing outlines around objects versus a bounding box and then classifying that object.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: What's the value of segmentation?

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: What is it as a problem in computer vision?

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: How is it fundamentally different from detection, recognition and the other problems?

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: Yeah, so I think so.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: So segmentation enables us to say that some set of pixels are an object without necessarily even being able to name that object or knowing properties of that object.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: So you mean segmentation purely as the act of separating an object from its background.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: A blob that's united in some way from its background.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: Yeah, so entitification, if you will, making an entity out of it.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: Entitification, beautifully.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: So I think that we have that capability and that enables us to, as we are growing up, to acquire names of objects with very little supervision.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: So suppose the child, let's posit that the child has this ability to separate out objects in the world.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: Then when the mother says, pick up your bottle or the cat's behaving funny today.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: The word cat suggests some object and then the child does the mapping.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: The mother doesn't have to teach specific object labels by pointing to them.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: Weak supervision works in the context that you have the ability to create objects.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: So I think that to me that's a very fundamental capability.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: There are applications where this is very important.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: For example, medical diagnosis.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: So in medical diagnosis, you have some brain scan.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: I mean, this is some work that we did in my group where you have CT scans of people who have had traumatic brain injury.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: And what the radiologist needs to do is to precisely delineate various places where there might be bleeds, for example.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: And there are clear needs like that.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: So there are certainly very practical applications of computer vision where segmentation is necessary.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: But philosophically, segmentation enables the task of recognition to proceed with much weaker supervision than we require today.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: And you think of segmentation as this kind of task that takes on a visual scene and breaks it apart into interesting entities that might be useful for whatever the task is.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: Yeah. And it is not semantics free.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: So I think it blends into, it involves perception and cognition.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: I think the mistake that we used to make in the early days of computer vision was to treat it as a purely bottom-up perceptual task.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: It is not just that.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: Because we do revise our notion of segmentation with more experience.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: Because, for example, there are objects which are non-rigid, like animals or humans.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: And I think understanding that all the pixels of a human are one entity is actually quite a challenge.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: Because the parts of the human, they can move independently.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: The human wears clothes, so they might be differently colored.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: So it is all sort of a challenge.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: You mentioned the three Rs of computer vision are recognition, reconstruction, reorganization.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: Can you describe these three Rs and how they interact?

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: Yeah. So recognition is the easiest one because that is what I think people generally think of as computer vision achieving these days, which is labels.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: So is this a cat? Is this a dog? Is this a chihuahua?

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: I mean, it could be very fine-grained, like a specific breed of a dog or a specific species of bird.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: Or it could be very abstract, like animal.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: But given a part of an image or a whole image, say, put a label on it.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: Yeah. So that's recognition.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: Reconstruction is essentially, you can think of it as inverse graphics.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: I mean, that's one way to think about it.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: So graphics is you have some internal computer representation and you have a computer representation of some objects arranged in a scene.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: And what you do is you produce a picture. You produce the pixels corresponding to a rendering of that scene.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: So let's do the inverse of this. We are given an image and we say, oh, this image arises from some objects in a scene looked at with a camera from this viewpoint.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: And we might have more information about the objects, like their shape, maybe their textures, maybe color, etc.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: So that's the reconstruction problem. In a way, you are in your head creating a model of the external world.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: Reorganization is to do with essentially finding these entities.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: So it's organization. The word organization implies structure.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: So in psychology, we use the term perceptual organization.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: That the world is not just an image is not just seen as is not internally represented as just a collection of pixels, but we make these entities. We create these entities, objects, whatever you want to call them.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: And the relationship between the entities as well? Or is it purely about the entities?

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: It could be about the relationships, but mainly we focus on the fact that there are entities.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: I'm trying to pinpoint what the organization means.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: So organization is that instead of like a uniform grid, we have this structure of objects.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: So segmentation is a small part of that.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: So segmentation gets us going towards that.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: Yeah. And you kind of have this triangle where they all interact together.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: Yes. So how do you see that interaction in sort of reorganization is yes, defining the entities in the world.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: The recognition is labeling those entities.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: And then reconstruction is what filling in the gaps?

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: Well, for example, see impute some 3D objects corresponding to each of these entities. That would be part of it.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: Adding more information that's not there in the raw data.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: Correct. I mean, I started pushing this kind of a view in the around 2010 or something like that.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: Because at that time in computer vision, the distinction that people were just working on many different problems,

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: but they treated each of them as a separate isolated problem with each with its own data set.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: And then you try to solve that and get good numbers on it.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: So I didn't like that approach because I wanted to see the connection between these.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: And if people divided up vision into various modules, the way they would do it is as low level, mid level and high level vision.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: Corresponding roughly to the psychologist's notion of sensation, perception and cognition.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: And that didn't map to tasks that people cared about.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: OK, so therefore I tried to promote this particular framework as a way of considering the problems that people in computer vision were actually working on

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: and trying to be more explicit about the fact that they actually are connected to each other.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: And I was at that time just doing this on the basis of information flow.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: Now it turns out in the last five years or so, in the post the deep learning revolution,

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: that this architecture has turned out to be very conducive to that.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: Because basically in these neural networks, we are trying to build multiple representations.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: There can be multiple output heads sharing common representations.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: So in a certain sense, today, given the reality of what solutions people have to these, I do not need to preach this anymore.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: It is just there. It's part of the solution space.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: So speaking of neural networks, how much of this problem of computer vision, of reorganization, recognition can be reconstruction?

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: How much of it can be learned end to end, do you think?

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: Sort of set it and forget it. Just plug and play.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: Have a giant data set, multiple, perhaps multimodal, and then just learn the entirety of it.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: Well, I think that currently what that end to end learning means nowadays is end to end supervised learning.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: And that I would argue is too narrow a view of the problem.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: I like this child development view, this lifelong learning view,

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: one where there are certain capabilities that are built up and then there are certain capabilities which are built up on top of that.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: So that's what I believe in.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: So I think end to end learning in the supervised setting for a very precise task to me is sort of a limited view of the learning process.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: Got it. So if we think about beyond purely supervised, look back to children.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: You mentioned six lessons that we can learn from children of being multimodal, being incremental, being physical, explore, be social, use language.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: Can you speak to these perhaps picking one that you find most fundamental to our time today?

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: Yeah. So I mean, I should say to give a due credit, this is from a paper by Smith and Gasser.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: And it reflects essentially, I would say, common wisdom among child development people.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: It's just that this is not common wisdom among people in computer vision and AI and machine learning.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: So I view my role as trying to bridge the two worlds.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: So let's take an example of a multimodal. I like that. So multimodal, a canonical example is a child interacting with an object.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: So then the child holds a ball and plays with it. So at that point, it's getting a touch signal.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: So the touch signal is getting the notion of 3D shape, but it is sparse.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: And then the child is also seeing a visual signal.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: And these two, so imagine these are two in totally different spaces.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: So one is the space of receptors on the skin of the fingers and the thumb and the palm.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: And then these map onto these neuronal fibers are getting activated somewhere.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: These lead to some activation in somatosensory cortex.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: I mean, a similar thing will happen if we have a robot hand.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: And then we have the pixels corresponding to the visual view, but we know that they correspond to the same object.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: So that's a very, very strong cross-calibration signal. And it is self-supervisory, which is beautiful.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: There's nobody assigning a label. The mother doesn't have to come and assign a label.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: The child doesn't even have to know that this object is called a ball.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: But the child is learning something about the three-dimensional world from this signal.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: I think tactile and visual, there is some work on. There is a lot of work currently on audio and visual.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: And audio-visual, so there is some event that happens in the world.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: And that event has a visual signature and it has an auditory signature.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: So there is this glass bowl on the table and it falls and breaks.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: And I hear the smashing sound and I see the pieces of glass.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: Okay, I've built that connection between the two.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: People, I mean, this has become a hot topic in computer vision in the last couple of years.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: There are problems like separating out multiple speakers, which was a classic problem in audition.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: They call this the problem of source separation or the cocktail party effect and so on.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: But just try to do it visually when you also have, it becomes so much easier and so much more useful.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: So the multimodal, I mean, there's so much more signal with multimodal and you can use that for some kind of weak supervision as well.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: Yes, because they are occurring at the same time in time.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: So you have time, which links the two.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: So at a certain moment, T1, you've got a certain signal in the auditory domain and a certain signal in the visual domain.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: But they must be causally related.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: That's an exciting area. Not well studied yet.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: Yeah, I mean, we have a little bit of work at this, but so much more needs to be done.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: So this is a good example.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: Do you think this is something we should be worried about or we need to first allow the unknown unknowns to become known unknowns?

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: I think we need to be worried about AI today. I think that it is not just a worry we need to have when we get that AGI.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: I think that AI is being used in many systems today. And there might be settings, for example, when it causes biases or decisions which could be harmful,

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: I mean, decisions which could be unfair to some people, or it could be self-driving cars which kills a pedestrian.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: So AI systems are being deployed today, right? And they are being deployed in many different settings, maybe in medical diagnosis, maybe in a self-driving car, maybe in selecting applicants for an interview.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: So I would argue that when these systems make mistakes, there are consequences, and we are in a certain sense responsible for those consequences.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: So I would argue that this is a continuous effort. And this is something that in a way is not so surprising.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: It's about all engineering and scientific progress, which great power comes great responsibility.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: So as these systems are deployed, we have to worry about them, and it's a continuous problem.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: I don't think of it as something which will suddenly happen on some day in 2079 for which I need to design some clever trick.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: I'm saying that these problems exist today, and we need to be continuously on the lookout for worrying about safety, biases, risks, right?

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: I mean, a self-driving car kills a pedestrian, and they have, right?

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: I mean, this Uber incident in Arizona, right? It has happened, right?

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: This is not about AGI. In fact, it's about a very dumb intelligence, which is still killing people.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: The worry people have with AGI is the scale. But I think you're 100% right.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: The thing that worries me about AI today, and it's happening on a huge scale, is recommender systems, recommendation systems.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: So if you look at Twitter, Facebook, or YouTube, they're controlling the ideas that we have access to, the news and so on.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: And that's a fundamentally machine learning algorithm behind each of these recommendations.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: And they, I mean, my life would not be the same without these sources of information.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: I'm a totally new human being, and the ideas that I know are very much because of the internet, because of the algorithms that recommend those ideas.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: And so as they get smarter and smarter, I mean, that is the AGI.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: The algorithm that's recommending the next YouTube video you should watch has control of millions of billions of people.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: That algorithm is already super intelligent and has complete control of the population.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: Not a complete, but very strong control. For now, we can turn off YouTube.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: We can just go have a normal life outside of that. But the more and more that gets into our life, it's that algorithm.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: We start depending on it in the different companies that are working on the algorithm.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: So I think it's, you're right, it's already there. And YouTube in particular is using computer vision,

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: doing their hardest to try to understand the content of videos so they could be able to connect videos with the people who would benefit from those videos the most.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: And so that development could go in a bunch of different directions, some of which might be harmful.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: So yeah, you're right. The threats of AI here already, we should be thinking about them.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: On a philosophical notion, if you could, personal perhaps, if you could relive a moment in your life outside of family,

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: because it made you truly happy or was a profound moment that impacted the direction of your life, what moment would you go to?

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: I don't think of single moments, but I look over the long haul.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: I feel that I've been very lucky because I feel that I think that in scientific research,

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: a lot of it is about being at the right place at the right time.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: And you can work on problems at a time when they're just too premature.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: You know, you butt your head against them and nothing happens because the prerequisites for success are not there.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: And then there are times when you are in a field which is all pretty mature and you can only solve curlicues upon curlicues.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: I've been lucky to have been in this field, which for 34 years, well, actually 34 years is a pretty long time.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: 34 years as a professor at Berkeley, so longer than that.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: Which when I started in it was just like some little crazy, absolutely useless field.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: Couldn't really do anything to a time when it's really, really solving a lot of practical problems.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: But I think that the field has offered a lot of tools for scientific research,

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: because computer vision is impactful for images in biology or astronomy and so on and so forth.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: And we have made great scientific progress, which has had real practical impact in the world.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: I got in at a time when the field was very young and at a time when it is now mature, but not fully mature.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: It's mature, but not done. I mean, it's really still in a productive phase.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: Yeah, I think people 500 years from now would laugh at you calling this field mature.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: That is very possible.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: But you also, lest I forget to mention, you've also mentored some of the biggest names of computer vision, computer science and AI today.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: There's so many questions I could ask, but really is, how did you do it?

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: What does it take to be a good mentor? What does it take to be a good guide?

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: Yeah, I think what I feel, I've been lucky to have had very, very smart and hardworking and creative students.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: I think some part of the credit just belongs to being at Berkeley.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: Those of us who are at top universities are blessed because we have very, very smart and capable students coming on knocking on our door.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: So I have to be humble enough to acknowledge that.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: But what have I added? I think I have added something.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: What I have added is, I think what I've always tried to teach them is a sense of picking the right problems.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: So I think that in science, in the short run, success is always based on technical competence.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: You're quick with math or you are whatever.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: I mean, there's certain technical capabilities which make for short range progress.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: Long range progress is really determined by asking the right questions and focusing on the right problems.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: And I feel that what I've been able to bring to the table in terms of advising these students is some sense of taste of what are good problems.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: What are problems that are worth attacking now as opposed to waiting 10 years?

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: What's a good problem? If you could summarize, is that possible to even summarize? What's your sense of a good problem?

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: I think I have a sense of what is a good problem, which is there is a British scientist.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: In fact, he won a Nobel Prize, Peter Medaver, who has a book on this.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: And basically, he calls it the research is the art of the soluble.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: So we need to sort of find problems which are not yet solved, but which are approachable.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: And he sort of refers to this sense that there is this problem which isn't quite solved yet, but it has a soft underbelly.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: There is some place where you can, you know, spear the beast.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: And having that intuition that this problem is ripe is a good thing, because otherwise you can just beat your head and not make progress.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: So I think that is important. So if I have that and if I can convey that to students,

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: it's not just that they do great research while they're working with me, but that they continue to do great research.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: So in a sense, I'm proud of my students and their achievements and their great research, even 20 years after they've ceased being my student.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: So it's in part developing, helping them develop that sense that a problem is not yet solved, but it's solvable.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: Correct. The other thing which I have, which I think I bring to the table is a certain intellectual breadth.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: I spend a fair amount of time studying psychology, neuroscience, relevant areas of applied math and so forth.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: So I can probably help them see some connections to disparate things, which they might not have otherwise.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: So the smart students coming into Berkeley can be very deep in the sense they can think very deeply,

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: meaning very hard down one particular path. But where I could help them is the shallow breadth,

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: but where they would have the narrow depth. But that's of some value.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: Well, it was beautifully refreshing just to hear you naturally jump to psychology, back to computer science, and this conversation back and forth.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: That's a rare quality. I think it's certainly for students empowering to think about problems in a new way.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jitendra Malik: Computer Vision | Lex Fridman Podcast #110

body.input: So for that and for many other reasons, I really enjoyed this conversation. Thank you so much. It was a huge honor. Thanks for talking to me.

body.input: It's been my pleasure.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Keras, Deep Learning, and the Progress of AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #38

body.input: Instead, what's making really long-term impact is very simple, very general systems

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Keras, Deep Learning, and the Progress of AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #38

body.input: that are really agnostic to all these tricks, because these tricks do not generalize.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Keras, Deep Learning, and the Progress of AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #38

body.input: And what's the shape of those concerns?

body.input: This is actually something I've briefly written about,

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Keras, Deep Learning, and the Progress of AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #38

body.input: but the capabilities of deep learning technology can be used in many ways

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Keras, Deep Learning, and the Progress of AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #38

body.input: that are concerning from mass surveillance with things like facial recognition,

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Keras, Deep Learning, and the Progress of AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #38

body.input: in general, tracking lots of data about everyone

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Keras, Deep Learning, and the Progress of AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #38

body.input: and then being able to making sense of this data, to do identification,

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Keras, Deep Learning, and the Progress of AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #38

body.input: to do prediction.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Keras, Deep Learning, and the Progress of AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #38

body.input: That's concerning.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Keras, Deep Learning, and the Progress of AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #38

body.input: That's something that's being very aggressively pursued by totalitarian states,

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Keras, Deep Learning, and the Progress of AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #38

body.input: like China.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Keras, Deep Learning, and the Progress of AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #38

body.input: One thing I am very much concerned about is that our lives are increasingly online,

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Keras, Deep Learning, and the Progress of AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #38

body.input: are increasingly digital, made of information consumption and information production,

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Keras, Deep Learning, and the Progress of AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #38

body.input: our digital footprint, I would say.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Keras, Deep Learning, and the Progress of AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #38

body.input: And if you absorb all of this data and you are in control of where you consume information,

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Keras, Deep Learning, and the Progress of AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #38

body.input: you know, social networks and so on, recommendation engines,

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Keras, Deep Learning, and the Progress of AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #38

body.input: then you can build a sort of reinforcement loop for human behavior.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Keras, Deep Learning, and the Progress of AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #38

body.input: You can observe the state of your mind at time t.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Keras, Deep Learning, and the Progress of AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #38

body.input: You can predict how you would react to different pieces of content,

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Keras, Deep Learning, and the Progress of AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #38

body.input: how to get you to move your mind in a certain direction.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Keras, Deep Learning, and the Progress of AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #38

body.input: And then you can feed you the specific piece of content that would move you in a specific direction.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Keras, Deep Learning, and the Progress of AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #38

body.input: And you can do this at scale, you know, at scale in terms of doing it continuously in real time.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Keras, Deep Learning, and the Progress of AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #38

body.input: You can also do it at scale in terms of scaling this to many, many people, to entire populations.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Keras, Deep Learning, and the Progress of AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #38

body.input: So potentially artificial intelligence, even in its current state,

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Keras, Deep Learning, and the Progress of AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #38

body.input: if you combine it with the Internet, with the fact that we have all of our lives are moving to digital devices

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Keras, Deep Learning, and the Progress of AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #38

body.input: and digital information consumption and creation,

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Keras, Deep Learning, and the Progress of AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #38

body.input: what you get is the possibility to achieve mass manipulation of behavior and mass psychological control.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Keras, Deep Learning, and the Progress of AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #38

body.input: And this is a very real possibility.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Keras, Deep Learning, and the Progress of AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #38

body.input: Yeah. So you're talking about any kind of recommender system.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Keras, Deep Learning, and the Progress of AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #38

body.input: Let's look at the YouTube algorithm, Facebook, anything that recommends content you should watch next.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Keras, Deep Learning, and the Progress of AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #38

body.input: And it's fascinating to think that there's some aspects of human behavior that you can, you know,

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Keras, Deep Learning, and the Progress of AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #38

body.input: say a problem of is this person hold Republican beliefs or Democratic beliefs?

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Keras, Deep Learning, and the Progress of AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #38

body.input: And it's a trivial, that's an objective function.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Keras, Deep Learning, and the Progress of AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #38

body.input: And you can optimize and you can measure and you can turn everybody into Republican.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Keras, Deep Learning, and the Progress of AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #38

body.input: Absolutely. Yeah. I do believe it's true.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Keras, Deep Learning, and the Progress of AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #38

body.input: So the human mind is very...

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Keras, Deep Learning, and the Progress of AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #38

body.input: If you look at the human mind as a kind of computer program, it has a very large exploit surface, right?

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Keras, Deep Learning, and the Progress of AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #38

body.input: It has many, many vulnerabilities.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Keras, Deep Learning, and the Progress of AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #38

body.input: Exploit surfaces, yeah.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Keras, Deep Learning, and the Progress of AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #38

body.input: Ways you can control it.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Keras, Deep Learning, and the Progress of AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #38

body.input: For instance, when it comes to your political beliefs, this is very much tied to your identity.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Keras, Deep Learning, and the Progress of AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #38

body.input: So for instance, if I'm in control of your news feed on your favorite social media platforms,

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Keras, Deep Learning, and the Progress of AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #38

body.input: this is actually where you're getting your news from.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Keras, Deep Learning, and the Progress of AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #38

body.input: And I can, of course, I can choose to only show you news that will make you see the world in a specific way, right?

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Keras, Deep Learning, and the Progress of AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #38

body.input: But I can also, you know, create incentives for you to post about some political beliefs.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Keras, Deep Learning, and the Progress of AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #38

body.input: I can just show it to people who will agree and they will like it.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Keras, Deep Learning, and the Progress of AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #38

body.input: And that will reinforce the statement in your mind.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Keras, Deep Learning, and the Progress of AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #38

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Keras, Deep Learning, and the Progress of AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #38

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Keras, Deep Learning, and the Progress of AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #38

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Keras, Deep Learning, and the Progress of AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #38

body.input: But maybe you will even, you know, stop believing this because you got pushback, right?

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Keras, Deep Learning, and the Progress of AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #38

body.input: So there are many ways in which social media platforms can potentially control your opinions.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Keras, Deep Learning, and the Progress of AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #38

body.input: And today, the...

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Keras, Deep Learning, and the Progress of AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #38

body.input: So all of these things are already being controlled by AI algorithms.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Keras, Deep Learning, and the Progress of AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #38

body.input: These algorithms do not have any explicit political goal today, while potentially they could.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Keras, Deep Learning, and the Progress of AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #38

body.input: Like if some totalitarian government takes over social media platforms and decides that, you know,

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Keras, Deep Learning, and the Progress of AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #38

body.input: now we are going to use this not just for mass surveillance, but also for mass opinion control and behavior control,

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Keras, Deep Learning, and the Progress of AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #38

body.input: very bad things could happen.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Keras, Deep Learning, and the Progress of AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #38

body.input: But what's really fascinating and actually quite concerning is that even without an explicit intent to manipulate,

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Keras, Deep Learning, and the Progress of AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #38

body.input: you're already seeing very dangerous dynamics in terms of how these content recommendation algorithms behave.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Keras, Deep Learning, and the Progress of AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #38

body.input: Because right now, the goal, the objective function of these algorithms is to maximize engagement, right?

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Keras, Deep Learning, and the Progress of AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #38

body.input: Which seems fairly innocuous at first, right?

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Keras, Deep Learning, and the Progress of AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #38

body.input: However, it is not because content that will maximally engage people, you know, get people to react in an emotional way,

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Keras, Deep Learning, and the Progress of AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #38

body.input: get people to click on something, it is very often content that, you know, is not healthy to the public discourse.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Keras, Deep Learning, and the Progress of AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #38

body.input: For instance, fake news are far more likely to get you to click on them than real news,

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Keras, Deep Learning, and the Progress of AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #38

body.input: simply because they are not constrained to reality.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Keras, Deep Learning, and the Progress of AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #38

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Keras, Deep Learning, and the Progress of AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #38

body.input: To me, that's an exciting world because so much good can come.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Keras, Deep Learning, and the Progress of AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #38

body.input: So there's an opportunity to educate people.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Keras, Deep Learning, and the Progress of AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #38

body.input: You can balance people's worldview with other ideas.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Keras, Deep Learning, and the Progress of AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #38

body.input: So there's so many objective functions.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Keras, Deep Learning, and the Progress of AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #38

body.input: The space of objective functions that create better civilizations is large, arguably infinite.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Keras, Deep Learning, and the Progress of AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #38

body.input: But there's also a large space that creates division and destruction, civil war, a lot of bad stuff.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Keras, Deep Learning, and the Progress of AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #38

body.input: And the worry is naturally, probably that space is bigger, first of all.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Keras, Deep Learning, and the Progress of AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #38

body.input: And if we don't explicitly think about what kind of effects are going to be observed from different objective functions,

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Keras, Deep Learning, and the Progress of AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #38

body.input: then we're going to get into trouble.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Keras, Deep Learning, and the Progress of AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #38

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Keras, Deep Learning, and the Progress of AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #38

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Keras, Deep Learning, and the Progress of AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #38

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Keras, Deep Learning, and the Progress of AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #38

body.input: I think you can definitely try.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Keras, Deep Learning, and the Progress of AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #38

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Keras, Deep Learning, and the Progress of AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #38

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Keras, Deep Learning, and the Progress of AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #38

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Keras, Deep Learning, and the Progress of AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #38

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Keras, Deep Learning, and the Progress of AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #38

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Keras, Deep Learning, and the Progress of AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #38

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Keras, Deep Learning, and the Progress of AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #38

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Keras, Deep Learning, and the Progress of AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #38
